card.thesis: This engine has no cross-symbol operator -- entry and exit are evaluated per instrument against that instrument's own bars only -- so 'rotation' here is produced entirely by the universe, the fixed fill order, and a 3-of-6 slot cap, not by any rule that compares one symbol to another. What the card does: apply one absolute filter (close above its own 100-day average, RSI(14) between 50 and 75 -- an established but not extended move) identically across six instruments split into two economically opposed legs: a defensive-equity leg (XLP staples, XLU utilities, XLV health care -- the three lowest-beta S&P sectors) and an energy/commodity reflation leg (XLE energy, DBC broad commodities, USO crude oil). Each leg is only ever held when its own trend is intact; the same filter drops a name the moment its trend breaks, with no view on what should happen next. I deliberately excluded Treasuries and gold from this universe -- the classic disinflation hedge -- because that basket (TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD) is already the field's `c14-riskmanaged-wide` card; building the same basket again under a different label would be one hypothesis wearing two names, which is exactly the redundancy Benjamini-Hochberg correction penalizes every other card for. This card instead answers a different question: which side of the value/defensive-versus-growth axis is actually confirmed in trend right now, given no ability to compare the two sides directly, only to filter each independently. The other side of these trades: momentum capital that stays concentrated in the AI/growth complex through a rotation because that is its mandate, not because it disagrees about the rotation; cross-asset traders who fade an energy or commodity breakout as 'a dead trade' and get run over by a multi-month reflation move (their mirror-image mistake is fading a defensive-sector rally as 'boring' and missing a growth-scare rotation); and momentum/CTA flow on the other side of whichever leg is currently exiting, since a slow, rule-following trend-break here is a late seller relative to a discretionary desk. I measured, through 2026-02-13: trailing 252-session correlation of each name's daily return to QQQ (used as a proxy for the AI/growth-momentum complex both B-momentum and C-trend trade) -- XLP 0.188, USO 0.270, DBC 0.342, XLU 0.397, XLV 0.430, XLE 0.509 -- mean 0.356, below the 0.57 the round's own brief measures between B-momentum and C-trend, though not as low as c14's near-zero figure, because equity-sector and energy exposure still carries real beta to broad risk sentiment that a pure bond/gold book does not. Breadth: on the 4,994 sessions since 2006-04-09 (all six symbols have data) where the entry filter is computable, a median of 3 of 6 and a mean of 2.78 of 6 qualify simultaneously; at least 3 qualify on 56.4% of sessions, so a 3-slot cap is a real, regularly binding constraint rather than a formality. When more than 3 qualify on the same session, the broker fills in the order below -- ascending by the same trailing correlation-to-QQQ measured above, so the names this round's own combined-book scoring cares most about (the ones least correlated to the incumbents) get filled first when a choice must be made. I am not claiming this ordering is itself a source of edge: the programme's own sensitivity test moved one card's three-year return across a 53.9-point spread (sigma 21.2) purely from re-ordering an identical universe, so any single-window margin this produces could be entirely inside that noise band, and I say so rather than dress an arbitrary-but-reasoned tiebreak up as a finding. None of these six names is selected because it is an S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 constituent, and none is a single-stock pick at all -- five are diversified sector or commodity ETF baskets and one (USO) tracks a single physical commodity future; the selection logic is asset-class role and measured correlation to the AI-momentum complex, not survivorship-adjacent index membership, so this card does not inherit the universe_knowable_from gate. I do flag honestly that the sector SPDRs' own internal holdings rebalance to track the present-day S&P 500's sector composition, which is a much weaker and indirect version of the same effect. Sized well under the book: 3 slots at 15% is a 45% maximum commitment, against the A-family's ~90% nominal (and ~0.47-0.49 realised) capital exposure that this discipline was retired for; a naive occupancy proxy (mean of min(qualifying,3) times 0.15 across the same history) comes to roughly 0.32, meaningfully below the A family's realised figure by construction, not by luck. What this does that passively holding the same six names would not: a static equal-weight holding of XLP/XLU/XLV/XLE/DBC/USO would have been long the energy/commodity leg all the way into its oil-2014 collapse and would have owned whichever leg is currently breaking down at all times; this card only ever holds a name while its own trend is intact, exits it on a trend break or a 10% stop (whichever comes first against the next session's open, since fills and stops both act on lagging prices, not the intraday low), and caps how much of the book any single regime call can consume. That is discipline over exposure, not prediction of direction -- it will lag every turn by design, and I say what that costs in the falsification section of the accompanying memo.
card.entry: close > sma(100) and rsi(14) > 50 and rsi(14) < 75
